posts.title: Physical AI, Explained: When Intelligence Leaves the Screen
posts.excerpt: Physical AI senses the real world, decides and acts through hardware. What makes it different from the AI you already use, where it is useful today, and the questions to ask before you start.
posts.content:
For most organisations, AI arrived as text: chatbots, copilots, tools that draft and summarise. Physical AI is a different kind of system. It senses the real world, decides what to do, and acts on it through hardware. NVIDIA describes it as AI that lets autonomous machines [perceive, understand and perform complex actions in the physical world](https://www.nvidia.com/en-gb/glossary/physical-ai/). IBM frames it more simply: [AI that operates in and interacts with the physical world](https://www.ibm.com/topics/physical-ai), not only in software.

That sounds like robotics with a new name, and partly it is. What has changed is how capable, affordable and practical these systems have become, and how much is now expected of them.

## How it differs from the AI you already use

The same underlying ideas power a chatbot and an autonomous inspection drone. Everything around them is different.

- Mistakes are physical. A wrong answer from a chatbot is an edit. A wrong decision from a machine is a collision, a spill or a missed event.
- Time is a hard constraint. Decisions often have to be made in milliseconds, on the device, without waiting for a server.
- The world does not follow the script. Lighting changes, weather moves in, sensors get dirty, people behave unpredictably.
- Good data is scarce. You cannot download examples of how your conveyor jams or how your site looks in a dust storm. You have to collect them.

## The building blocks

Every physical AI system, from a warehouse robot to a perimeter sensor, is built from the same layers.

- Perception: cameras, thermal imagers, LiDAR, radar and motion sensors that turn the world into data.
- Understanding: models that detect, track and estimate what is happening and where.
- Decision: planning what to do next, within limits that keep the system safe.
- Action: motors, actuators, alerts or instructions to an operator.
- The loop around it: simulation before deployment, testing in real conditions, monitoring in service, and safe updates.

The model is usually the smallest part of the work. The sensors, power, enclosure, safety limits and operations around it decide whether the system actually works.

## Why now

Three things have matured at the same time. Models generalise better than they did a few years ago, so they need less hand-tuning for each new environment. Compute that can run them on a small, low-power device is far more affordable. And simulation tools now let teams test thousands of scenarios before a machine ever leaves the workshop.

Adoption shows it. The International Federation of Robotics reports that the number of industrial robots in operation worldwide reached [a record 5 million in 2025](https://ifr.org/news/five-million-robots-now-operate-in-factories-globally/), with more than 600,000 installed that year alone. Most of that growth is concentrated in a few markets, led by China. Africa is barely on the map yet, which is exactly why it is worth thinking about now.

## Where it is useful today, beyond humanoids

Humanoid robots get the headlines. Most of the value sits in less glamorous places.

- Inspection: drones and crawlers that check power lines, pipelines, telecom towers and solar farms, so people do not have to climb or travel to every asset.
- Agriculture: crop monitoring, early detection of disease and pests, and precise spraying.
- Logistics: counting, sorting and tracking stock in warehouses and yards.
- Monitoring large sites: perimeters, ports and coastlines, where the area is too large for people to watch continuously.
- Quality control: computer vision that catches defects on a production line before they reach a customer.

## The West African angle

In much of West Africa, the case for physical AI is less about replacing labour and more about reach, safety and consistency. Assets are spread over long distances, some sites are hard or dangerous to reach, and checks that depend on someone being in the right place at the right time are easy to miss.

The constraints are local too. Heat, dust, unreliable power and patchy connectivity break systems that were designed and tested somewhere else. We look at that in detail in [Edge AI in Heat, Dust and Patchy Connectivity](/blog/edge-ai-west-african-conditions).

## Questions to ask before you start

- What decision will the machine make, and what happens when it gets it wrong?
- Where will the computing happen: on the device, at a local site, or in the cloud? What happens when the link drops?
- What does it need to see, and in what conditions: night, rain, glare, dust?
- How will it be tested before it meets the real world?
- Who maintains it, cleans it, and updates it once it is in service?
- Would a simpler, non-AI solution do the job well enough?

That last question matters most. The best physical AI projects start from a clear operational problem, not from the technology.

## Our view

Physical AI is engineering, not magic. The organisations that benefit from it will be the ones that treat it as a complete system, designed for their own conditions, with safety and maintenance planned from the first day. If you are weighing where it could fit in your operations, we are happy to [talk it through in confidence](/contact).

## Sources

- [What Is Physical AI? (NVIDIA)](https://www.nvidia.com/en-gb/glossary/physical-ai/)
- [What is physical AI? (IBM)](https://www.ibm.com/topics/physical-ai)
- [Five million robots now operate in factories globally (International Federation of Robotics, World Robotics 2026)](https://ifr.org/news/five-million-robots-now-operate-in-factories-globally/)

posts.title: Edge AI in Heat, Dust and Patchy Connectivity: Designing for West African Conditions
posts.excerpt: Most edge AI is built for air-conditioned labs with stable power and fast internet. Here is what changes when it has to work in heat, Harmattan dust, power cuts and patchy coverage.
posts.content:
Most edge AI is designed in air-conditioned rooms with stable power and fast internet. Then it is installed somewhere hot, dusty and remote, with neither. The model that scored well in the lab starts missing detections, the device restarts at random, and nobody can reach it to find out why.

None of this is unique to West Africa, but conditions here expose every shortcut. These are the four things we design for from the start.

## Heat: the silent performance killer

Accra's average daily high sits above 32°C from January to April, according to [long-term climate records](https://bluegreenatlas.com/climate/ghana_climate.html), and it is hotter inland. Inside a sealed enclosure in direct sun, the temperature the electronics experience is far higher than the air around it.

Many popular development kits are not built for that. NVIDIA, for example, specifies the carrier board of its Jetson Orin Nano developer kit for [an operating range of 0°C to 35°C](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/jetson-orin-nano-super-dev-kit-survival-and-operating-temperature/370802). Industrial modules exist for harsher conditions: the Jetson AGX Orin Industrial is rated for [-40°C to 85°C at its thermal transfer plate](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/1913/0443/files/jetson-orin-datasheet-jetson-agx-orin-industrial-web-nv-us-2757128-r2.pdf).

The danger is not only failure. When a processor gets too hot it slows itself down to protect itself. The system keeps running, but the frame rate drops and detections are quietly missed. Nothing looks broken until something important is missed.

- Choose compute rated for the conditions, not just the benchmark.
- Shade the enclosure, use light, reflective finishes, and give heat a passive path out.
- Run models with headroom, so a slower processor still keeps up.
- Test at worst-case temperatures, in the enclosure, in the sun.
- Report temperature and throttling in telemetry, so slowdowns are visible.

## Dust, humidity and salt

From roughly December to March, the Harmattan carries Saharan dust across the region, at times [cutting visibility to around a kilometre](https://www.worldtravelguide.net/guides/africa/ghana/weather-climate-geography). Dust clogs fans, coats lenses and wears moving parts. On the coast, humidity typically runs [between about 73% and 85%](https://www.weather-atlas.com/en/ghana/accra-climate), and salt air corrodes connectors.

Enclosure ratings give a common language for this. Under the IEC 60529 standard, the first digit of an IP rating covers dust and the second covers water: [IP65 is dust-tight and protected against water jets, IP67 survives temporary immersion](https://www.newark.com/es/applications-harsh-environments-ingress-protection-ip-ratings).

- Aim for dust-tight, sealed enclosures, and avoid open fans where possible.
- Protect lenses with hoods and coatings, and plan who cleans them and how often.
- Use corrosion-resistant connectors and protective coatings near the coast.
- Train and validate vision models on hazy, dusty and low-light images from the actual site. Models trained on clear-weather data degrade when the air does.

## Power: assume it will fail

Unreliable power is a design input, not an exception. A 2024 survey by the Institute of Economic Affairs found that [about 94% of respondents in Greater Accra experienced outages, from once to more than seven times a week](https://www.myjoyonline.com/dumsor-brought-untold-hardship-to-most-people-in-the-gt-accra-region-iea-survey/), and that 70.7% of businesses reported major or severe effects.

- Protect against surges and unstable voltage, not just outages.
- Add battery backup sized for the outages you expect, and solar where it makes sense.
- Shut down cleanly when power is running out, and use storage and file systems that survive sudden power loss.
- Recover automatically on boot, with watchdogs that restart anything that hangs.

## Connectivity: design offline-first

According to the GSMA, Sub-Saharan Africa still has the [largest mobile broadband coverage gap of any region, at around 10% of the population](https://www.connectivity.technology/2025/10/the-state-of-mobile-internet-coverage.html), and the gap between urban and rural areas is wide. Even where there is coverage, bandwidth and reliability vary through the day.

A system that depends on the cloud to make decisions will fail exactly when it matters.

- Run inference on the device, and make the important decisions locally.
- Send events, not video streams: a detection, a timestamp, a small image.
- Queue data when the link is down, and send it when it returns.
- Make updates resumable, verified and reversible, so a dropped connection never leaves a device broken.
- Keep local alerting working without the cloud.

## A short checklist

- Compute rated for real temperatures, tested in its enclosure.
- Temperature and throttling visible in telemetry.
- A dust-tight enclosure, with a cleaning plan.
- Training and validation data from local conditions.
- Power protection, backup and clean recovery.
- Offline-first behaviour, sending events instead of streams.
- Safe remote updates with rollback.
- A named owner for maintenance once the system is in service.

## The point

The hardware and models are global. The conditions are local. Systems that work here are designed for here from the first day, not adapted after the first failure. For the bigger picture, read [Physical AI, Explained](/blog/physical-ai-explained), or [talk to us in confidence](/contact) about your own environment.

## Sources

- [Climate data for Accra (Blue Green Atlas)](https://bluegreenatlas.com/climate/ghana_climate.html)
- [Jetson Orin Nano developer kit operating temperature (NVIDIA Developer Forums)](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/jetson-orin-nano-super-dev-kit-survival-and-operating-temperature/370802)
- [Jetson AGX Orin Industrial datasheet (NVIDIA)](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/1913/0443/files/jetson-orin-datasheet-jetson-agx-orin-industrial-web-nv-us-2757128-r2.pdf)
- [Ghana weather, climate and geography (World Travel Guide)](https://www.worldtravelguide.net/guides/africa/ghana/weather-climate-geography)
- [Accra climate (Weather Atlas)](https://www.weather-atlas.com/en/ghana/accra-climate)
- [Ingress Protection (IP) Ratings, IEC 60529 (Newark)](https://www.newark.com/es/applications-harsh-environments-ingress-protection-ip-ratings)
- [IEA survey on power outages in Greater Accra (MyJoyOnline)](https://www.myjoyonline.com/dumsor-brought-untold-hardship-to-most-people-in-the-gt-accra-region-iea-survey/)
- [The State of Mobile Internet Coverage and Infrastructure 2025, on the GSMA report (Connectivity Technology)](https://www.connectivity.technology/2025/10/the-state-of-mobile-internet-coverage.html)

posts.title: Why Enterprise Software Projects Take Twice as Long as They Should — And How We Fixed It
posts.excerpt: The average enterprise software project runs 45% over schedule. Most vendors blame complexity. We blame process. Here's how an architecture-first method removes most of that delay.
posts.content:
The Standish Group's Chaos Report and similar studies have confirmed what every CTO already knows: the average enterprise software project runs roughly 45% over schedule. Budget overruns and missed deadlines are so common they're almost expected. Most vendors point to complexity: integration challenges, legacy systems, shifting requirements. We see it differently. The problem isn't complexity alone; it's how work is structured. This article explains our approach and why it removes most of that delay while maintaining the quality required for mission-critical software development.

## Where Time Actually Goes

The dirty secret of slow software projects is that the delays rarely happen during development. They happen before it.

Vague or shifting requirements mean teams build, then rebuild. Architecture decisions made during sprint planning instead of before coding lead to rework when the system doesn't scale or integrate. Communication gaps between stakeholders and engineers result in surprises at demo time. The single biggest cost is building the wrong thing right: polishing features that get cut or reimagined later.

In a typical project timeline, weeks disappear into clarification cycles, change requests, and scope creep. Development only starts after partial alignment, so every subsequent change is expensive. In our model, we front-load discovery and design. We invest in stakeholder interviews, technical audits, and a system design document that acts as a contract before a single line of production code is written. That compresses the overall arc: less rework, fewer revisions, and a project that ends on the date we quoted.Timelines are set in discovery and planned milestone by milestone.

## The Architecture-First Method

We design the full system before writing production code. This isn't a new idea. In aerospace and defense engineering, it's standard practice. Commercial software has largely abandoned it in favor of "move fast" culture. We've brought it back.

Technical discovery comes first: stakeholder interviews, infrastructure audits, constraint mapping. We capture requirements, risks, and success criteria in a structured way. Then we produce a system design document, agreed upon with the client before development begins. That document acts as the single source of truth. It defines components, interfaces, data flows, and non-functional requirements. QA criteria and test scenarios are defined at the design phase, not after launch. When development starts, there's no ambiguity about what "done" looks like.

This approach eliminates the back-and-forth that kills velocity. There are no surprise demos where stakeholders see something for the first time and request major changes. Design reviews happen when changes are cheap. The result is faster enterprise software delivery without compromise on quality or scope. If you're evaluating how long software development should take for your next build, the answer depends heavily on whether your vendor front-loads design or wings it.

## The Role of Dedicated Teams

Context switching is the silent killer of software timelines. When engineers split their attention across three or four projects, velocity collapses. Meetings multiply. "Let me catch up on where we left off" becomes a tax on every sprint. We assign dedicated teams to engagements. The result is sustained focus, faster decision-making, and no catch-up tax. For mission-critical software development, that focus isn't optional; it's how you reduce software project timeline and hit dates.

## What This Means for You

If you're a CTO or VP of Engineering evaluating vendors, the practical implications are straightforward. You'll have fewer status meetings, because the system design document does the communicating. You'll get shorter feedback loops: design reviews instead of surprise demos. And you'll get a project that ends on the date we quoted. Every engagement gets a milestone-by-milestone plan before development begins. That's not a pitch; it's the outcome of a process built to remove the variables that cause overruns.

## Close

If your last software project ran over schedule, it wasn't bad luck. It was a process problem. Our process is designed to remove that variable. If you're evaluating vendors for a mission-critical build, we'd be glad to walk you through exactly how we'd approach your project. Request a private briefing and we'll show you the playbook.

posts.title: What Defense-Grade Engineering Principles Can Teach Commercial Software Teams
posts.excerpt: The practices used in defense and intelligence software (redundancy, failure-mode analysis, security-first architecture) should be baseline for any business-critical commercial system. Most commercial software ignores them. Here's what that costs you.
posts.content:
Engineering culture in defense and intelligence is built around a simple premise: systems cannot afford to fail. Redundancy, threat modeling, and documentation discipline aren't optional; they're how projects are run. In commercial software, those practices are often treated as overhead. The gap between the two worlds is costly. This article outlines what commercial teams can learn from defense-grade engineering and what happens when business-critical systems are built to that standard.

## The Gap Between Defense and Commercial Engineering

In classified and government-adjacent work, requirements are locked down early. Failure modes are analyzed before build. Documentation is maintained so that systems can be audited and handed off. Security isn't bolted on at the end; it's designed in from the start. In many commercial environments, the opposite is true: speed is prioritized over resilience, and "we'll document it later" becomes never. The result is systems that work until they don't, and when they fail, the cost is measured in downtime, data exposure, and lost trust.

## Three Principles Commercial Teams Rarely Follow

Three principles from defense engineering should be baseline for any mission-critical commercial system.

Redundancy: Critical paths have backups. Single points of failure are identified and eliminated. That doesn't mean overbuilding: it means designing for failure so that when a component goes down, the system degrades gracefully instead of collapsing.

Threat modeling: Before coding, teams ask what can go wrong. Who might attack the system? What data is at risk? What happens if a dependency fails? Threat modeling surfaces risks early, when they're cheap to address.

Documentation discipline: Runbooks, architecture decisions, and operational procedures are kept current. When something breaks at 3 a.m., the on-call engineer isn't guessing. Audit trails and design docs make it possible to maintain and evolve systems long after the original team has moved on.

## What Happens When Commercial Systems Are Built to Defense Standards

When commercial systems are built with these principles, the outcomes are measurable. Uptime improves because failures are anticipated and mitigated. Resilience increases because redundancy and failover are designed in. Audit-readiness becomes straightforward: compliance and security reviews are easier when the architecture and documentation are already in place. For fintech, healthtech, legal, and other regulated industries, that's not a nice-to-have; it's the cost of doing business.

## How to Ask Your Vendor the Right Questions

If you're evaluating a vendor for a business-critical or mission-critical build, ask how they handle failure. Do they do threat modeling? How do they document architecture and operational procedures? Do they assign dedicated teams so that context isn't lost across projects? The answers will tell you whether you're getting defense-grade engineering or something that will "move fast" until it breaks. At The Trust Group, we build to the same standards for commercial clients as defense engineering demands, because the stakes are just as high.
